studies.title: A Band That Listened In
studies.meaning: The opening is a command to report, not to argue. Everything after the first clause is somebody else's speech, quoted. The listeners' reaction arrives in three moves: first an aesthetic judgement, that what they heard was astonishing; then a moral one, that it points toward sound conduct; then a creedal one, that their Lord has no partner, no consort and no child. Nothing is said about how they were persuaded. The order of the three is the argument.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the later years of the Meccan mission. The classical sources place the episode on a journey out of Mecca and differ over the route and the halt. They also differ over whether the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was aware of the listeners at the time, some reporting that he learned of the whole incident only when this surah came, others reporting a later meeting. The disagreement is old and neither side treats it as closed.

keyTerms.note: The word names a group of men small enough to count, a scouting party rather than a crowd. Choosing it keeps the episode modest: not a nation converted, a handful who happened to be within earshot.

An indefinite noun standing as a description, so the sense is closer to a recitation that is wonder itself. It marks surprise at something unclassifiable rather than approval of something already understood.
The root covers maturity and good sense, the opposite of being reckless with your own interests. It returns three more times in this surah, which makes it the note the whole speech keeps sounding.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Jinn were not a theological abstraction in Mecca. They were part of ordinary explanation: a poet's sudden gift, a man's unaccountable speech, a traveller who lost the road at night. Tribes camping in an unfamiliar valley are reported to have called aloud on its jinn for safety before sleeping, the way you would hobble a camel. So a report that some of them had stopped to listen landed in a world where their existence needed no defending.
studies.didYouKnow: The imperative to speak occurs five times in this surah. Once at the very start, opening the report of what the listeners said, and four times in the last nine ayat, where every one of them introduces something the Prophet does not know or does not control. The surah is framed at both ends by instructions on what to say.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Three denials are placed at the head of the surah and they are made by speakers outside the human quarrel: no consort, no child, no partner. Putting the most contested Meccan claim in the mouths of listeners with no stake in Meccan politics lifts it out of the tribal argument it had become. It also establishes that the recitation carries to hearers it was not addressed to, and that hearing it once, in passing, was enough.

crossReferences.why: Tells the same kind of episode from outside, with the group arriving, falling silent, and going home.
Gives the same denial of consort and child as the entire content of a surah.
Asks directly how God could have a child when there is no consort.

studies.applyIt: Find a recitation you have never heard: a reciter you do not know, or a surah you rarely reach. Listen to two minutes of it without the translation in front of you. The band in this passage judged what they heard before they had worked out all of it. Notice what your ear does on its own, and only then read what it said.

studies.title: We Never Thought Anyone Would Lie
studies.meaning: This is an account of how they were misled, and it is an admission about credulity rather than about malice. They had assumed nobody would dare invent a claim about God, so extravagant things said among them passed unchallenged. The word rendered as their fool is singular with a possessive attached, and commentators read it either as one figure or as a collective. The last sentence turns to the speakers' own people and tells them their assumption about resurrection was shared by those now confessing they were wrong.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The quoted speech belongs, in the classical accounts, to the moment the listeners returned to their own kind and gave their report. The setting behind it is a peninsula where claims about God circulated without any means of testing them, and where specialists in hidden knowledge made a living. No specific occasion is reported for these particular sentences beyond the episode the surah opens with.

keyTerms.note: The root names recklessness with what matters, the man judged unfit to hold property or speak for a clan. The form is singular and possessive, so the speakers are claiming the folly as belonging to them.
The noun means going far past a boundary, used of a price beyond reason or a claim beyond evidence. It is not the word for a lie but for a statement that has overshot what anyone could know.
The verb of taking shelter under a protector, and the same root as the Quran's own formula for seeking refuge with God. Pointing it at other creatures is exactly what makes the report pointed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Before sleeping in a strange valley, a traveller would call aloud on whoever was thought to command its jinn and ask for a quiet night. The early sources record this as an unremarkable precaution. In the towns, soothsayers sold a version of the same service, each claiming an informant who caught news from above, and fees rose with reputation. Somebody was always paying for access to what could not be checked.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for seeking refuge in the third of these ayat shares its root with the opening word of the last two surahs of the Quran. Those two are the only surahs built entirely as a request for protection, and the final one names jinn among the things a person shelters from. The vocabulary is identical; the direction is reversed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Error is located in a social mechanism rather than in a wicked heart. A community assumed a floor of honesty about God, somebody spoke below it, and nobody thought to check. That makes credulity a moral matter and not a misfortune. The denial of resurrection is then placed in the mouths of speakers who have since discovered otherwise, so the point is carried by testimony rather than by proof, which is how most of this surah works.

crossReferences.why: Shows angels disowning those who had in fact been worshipping jinn, answering the practice described here.
Names human and jinn adversaries who prompt one another with ornamented speech meant to deceive.
A whole surah given to seeking refuge, using the verb this passage reports being misdirected.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you believe about God, or about religion, that you have never traced to a source. You absorbed it from a relative, a speaker, something you scrolled past. Name it today, out loud or on paper, and go and find where it came from. The speakers here were not deceived by strangers. They were let down by never asking.

studies.title: We Do Not Know Which
studies.meaning: The report describes a change noticed from outside. Something they had always been able to do was suddenly closed, they went to investigate, and they found the sky under guard. What happens next is the unusual part: they draw no conclusion at all. They state plainly that they cannot tell whether the change means harm for the people of the earth or good for them, and the sentence stops. Commentators note the care of the grammar, which leaves the harm without an agent and names God only with the good.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, belonging to the period after the first revelations. The early sources connect the barring of the heavens with the beginning of the Quran's descent, so the investigation follows the interruption rather than explaining it. Accounts place the search on a journey out of Mecca toward the eastern market fairs and differ on the details of the route. What they agree on is the order of events, which is what the passage itself reports.

keyTerms.note: A verb of searching by hand rather than by sight, the way you feel along a wall in the dark. Applied to the sky, it makes the investigation sound physical and blind instead of learned.
The singular names a stick pulled burning from a fire. It is the same word Moses uses when he hopes to fetch a light from the fire he has seen, so its ordinary sense is a torch, not a weapon.
A word from the vocabulary of ambush, used of a watcher posted on a road. It turns the flame from an accident of the night sky into something stationed deliberately, with a purpose and a position.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Shooting stars were a common sight with a common explanation. People watched the sky as a matter of course, since travel and planting both depended on the stars, and a sudden streak across it was read as a missile thrown at something. Meteor showers were noticed and dated by the year they fell. The passage assumes an audience who had all stood outside at night and seen this, and tells them what they had been watching.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran describes the guarding of the sky in more than one place, but only here is it reported by the ones it was aimed at. Elsewhere the scene is given from outside, as a general account of what awaits an eavesdropper. Here the eavesdroppers narrate it themselves, in the past tense, as a change in their own working conditions.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The refusal to interpret is the point. Creatures with more reach than any human being, able to get to the edge of the heavens, arrive at a limit and say they do not know. Knowledge is bounded for everything made, not only for people. And the way they phrase the two possibilities, leaving harm unassigned while naming God with the good, models an instinct about how to speak of Him when the outcome has not arrived.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same guarded sky from outside, as what happens to any listener who tries to snatch a word.
Presents the guarding of the heavens as a standing arrangement rather than a recent change.
Lists what no creature knows, closing on the same honest admission of a limit.

studies.applyIt: Take the thing you are most uncertain about this week: a result, a diagnosis, a decision someone else is making about you. Say one sentence about it the way these speakers do. Not that it will turn out well, and not that it will not. Only that you do not know which of the two it is. Notice how much steadier that sentence is to hold than either of the others.

studies.title: Roads Torn Into Strips
studies.meaning: Three admissions in sequence, each narrower than the last. First, that their own kind is mixed and divided, with no single verdict available about them. Then, that the division changes nothing about the one fact that matters, since there is no ground anywhere on which God can be outrun. Then the turn, which is the only place in the whole speech where belief is described as happening. The result is stated as a subtraction: two named fears removed, rather than a reward held out.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the stretch when the believers in Mecca were few and under pressure, and were being told that the message had a reach they could not see. The classical accounts place this speech at the point where the listeners returned to their own people. They report the journey and differ on its route, and they attach no separate occasion to these particular sentences.

keyTerms.note: The second word names something torn lengthwise into strips, the way a hide is cut. The phrase pictures one road shredded rather than several roads deliberately laid, which makes division sound like damage.
The verb means to leave a pursuer helpless, to render him incapable. It belongs to chase and contest, so the denial is not about power in the abstract but about any escape actually working.

The word for being underpaid, used of a price cut below what is owed; it is the word for what Joseph was sold at. Set beside a term for being overburdened, it names the two ways a person gets cheated.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Roads out of Mecca were neither safe nor anonymous. A man who had wronged his clan could ride for days and still meet somebody who knew his father's name, and pursuit across open country was a practical trade with trackers who read prints in sand. Getting away meant reaching a protector before the trackers reached you. The middle admission here borrows that entire picture and removes only the destination.
studies.didYouKnow: Twelve consecutive ayat of this surah, from the third to the fourteenth, open with the same two-word construction: a conjunction and a particle meaning roughly and that. The run is what gives the speech its texture. It reads less like a story being told than like a list of statements being entered one after another, each standing on its own.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Division is described without being resolved. The speakers do not claim their people are good, and they do not condemn them; they say the community runs in strips and leave it there. What unifies is not their character but their position, since nowhere is outside. The final clause then gives belief a modest and precise effect. It does not promise that nothing will be lost, only that two particular fears stop operating.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for a cut-down price, in the sale of Joseph, which fixes its everyday sense.
Denies the same two escapes, distance on the earth and a set of backers, to the same audience.
States the impossibility of distance from God from the opposite side: He is nearer than the jugular vein.

studies.applyIt: Notice the two fears this passage names as leaving: being shortchanged, and being loaded with more than your share. Both are about fairness, not about pain. Think of one place you are quietly keeping accounts against somebody, waiting to be paid back. Say the account out loud to yourself once. Then decide whether you are going to keep holding it.

studies.title: Among Us Are Those Who Submit
studies.meaning: The division named here is not between kinds of creature but between kinds of response, and it repeats the shape of a sentence three ayat earlier about who among them is righteous. The name given to the second group has occupied commentators, because the root turns on a hair: this participle means one who swerves off the balance, while a form almost identical to it means one who deals justly. The verb applied to the first group is unusual too. They are said to have searched out and aimed at right conduct, not to have arrived at it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The speech closes here, at the point where the speakers sort their own community rather than describing what happened to them. The setting is a Mecca in which the message was dividing households and clans along exactly this line, between those who accepted and those who held their position, and the surah lets a non-human community report the same split from its own side.

keyTerms.note: The active participle of handing a thing over entire. Used here by speakers describing themselves, it shows the word working as a description of posture well before it settled into the name of a community.

From a root that also yields the word for dealing justly; the two participles differ by a single formal feature and mean opposite things. Arabic grammarians treat the pair as a standing example of that reversal.
The verb means to search deliberately for the best of something, the way you would pick the soundest fruit from a heap. It describes intent and effort, not a result already secured.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Handing yourself over was a recognised act with a public form. A man who had lost a fight, or whose clan could no longer carry him, went to another man and gave his person into that man's keeping, and the transfer was witnessed and complete. It was not a feeling about anything. It was a change in who answered for you and who would be asked to pay if you did harm.
studies.didYouKnow: The participle for those who submit appears across the Quran in the mouths of very different speakers: Abraham praying over the foundations of a house, Joseph asking to die that way, the disciples of Jesus answering him, sorcerers who had just changed sides in front of a king. Each time it is a self-description at a moment of decision, never a label applied from outside.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The dividing line is made identical for every kind of creature that hears. Neither the nature of these speakers nor their access to places people cannot reach counts for anything; only the response does. And by crediting the first group with aiming at right conduct rather than possessing it, the ayah keeps submission from hardening into a status. It stays the direction a creature is facing when the message arrives.

crossReferences.why: Shows the same group urging their own people toward the acceptance described here.
Puts the same self-description in the mouths of the disciples of Jesus at a moment of decision.
States the same fork, belief or refusal, and leaves it standing open in front of the hearer.

studies.applyIt: Look at the verb used of the ones who got it right. They aimed. Pick something you have been treating as settled about yourself, patient or honest or generous, and instead of coasting on the label, do one small deliberate thing in that direction today. Choose the harder option once. The ayah credits nobody with having arrived.

studies.title: Water Given As A Test
studies.meaning: The middle sentence is the surprising one. Abundance is named as what steadfastness would have produced, and then, in the very next breath, called a trial rather than a reward. Commentators differ on who is being spoken of, whether the sentence is still about the listeners of the earlier ayat or has turned to the people of Mecca, and on whether the water is rain or a figure for plenty in general. What they do not differ about is the structure: the gift and the test are the same object.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Drought belongs to the setting. The Meccan surahs return again and again to rain as the plainest evidence of dependence, and the sources describe hard years in the valley during the mission. Early commentators read the promise of abundant water against that background, some taking it as rain withheld from people who refused the message, others as a general statement of what steadfastness would have brought.

keyTerms.note: Gathered brushwood rather than timber. The word names fuel collected by hand to feed someone else's fire, and that is what makes the image demeaning as well as frightening.
Used of water that runs plentifully and keeps running. It occurs once in the entire Quran, and it describes a supply that does not stop rather than a single good rainfall.
From the root for climbing. It pictures punishment as an ascent that keeps getting harder, which matches the ayah's treatment of turning away as a direction rather than a single act.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca had no river and no farmland. Water came from wells, and a right to draw from one was a form of wealth that clans fought over and poets boasted about. A season of good rain filled the wadis and the grazing; a season without it meant selling stock and going into debt at rates that took years to clear. To an audience like that, the promise in the middle of this passage was not a metaphor about blessing. It named the thing they prayed for.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for abundant water in the second of these ayat occurs exactly once in the Quran. The Quran otherwise has a large vocabulary for rain, with separate words for the first light fall, the heavy downpour and the cloud that carries it. The one term reserved for a supply that simply keeps flowing is spent on a blessing that was not given.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Abundance is cut loose from approval. Water would have come as a consequence of holding the path, and the following ayah says outright that its purpose would have been to test them with it. That leaves the reader unable to read their own circumstances in either direction. Ease is not a verdict. The passage then places the real danger somewhere else entirely, in turning away from remembrance rather than in any external loss.

crossReferences.why: Promises the opening of the sky's blessings to a town that believes and is mindful, from the other direction.
Ties abundant rain to seeking forgiveness, spoken by Noah to a people who refused.
Shows plenty given to people who had forgotten, and then withdrawn, as the same kind of test.

studies.applyIt: Think of the easiest part of your life at the moment: the thing going well without you working at it. Sit for one minute with the idea that it is an examination rather than a verdict. Then name one specific way it could quietly go wrong for you. This is the reading the passage asks for, and it is steadier than gratitude on its own.

studies.title: The Ground Belongs To God
studies.meaning: The first sentence has been read several ways and the commentators record the range without settling it: the buildings where people prostrate, the sanctuary at Mecca in particular, or the parts of the body that touch the ground in prostration. Every reading arrives at the same instruction, that the act has one recipient. The scene that follows is deliberately unattributed. Somebody stood praying and a crowd pressed in so densely they almost piled on top of him, and the passage never says who the crowd was.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Public prayer in Mecca was conspicuous and provocative, and the sources describe the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) praying near the sanctuary and being obstructed, mocked and physically crowded. Commentators split over the crowd in the second of these ayat. Some read it as listeners pressing forward to hear the recitation; others as opponents massing against him. Both readings are early and neither is treated as decided.

keyTerms.note: A plural naming the place where an action happens, built from the verb to prostrate. It means the ground beneath a forehead before it ever means a building, which is why the classical readings spread so far.
From a root for wool pounded into felt. The picture is bodies compacted with no air between them. The Quran uses the root once more, of wealth piled into a heap by a man boasting about it.
The passage names him by service rather than by name. In a surah crowded with contested claims about God having a family, calling the Prophet a servant is doing quiet and deliberate work.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The sanctuary at Mecca was a crowded working space, not a quiet one. Pilgrims circled it, traders set up around its edges, and the idols of many tribes stood in and about the building, each with its own visitors and its own custodians drawing income. Prayer there happened in full view of people with money in the arrangement. A man praying to one God alone in that courtyard was making a claim about everybody else's business.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing the crowd here comes from the root that gives Arabic its word for felt, the cloth made by beating wool until it becomes a single mass. The Quran uses that root in exactly one other place, where a man boasts of having squandered wealth piled up in heaps. Both times the image is of quantity pressed together until it has no separate parts.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The instruction is framed as a property claim before it is framed as a prohibition. The ground of prostration belongs to God, so calling on anyone else while standing on it is a trespass rather than a mere error of judgement. And the closing ayah, handed to the Prophet as words to speak, keeps him inside the same rule as everyone else. He is shown praying, not being prayed to, in a surah that reports unseen creatures listening to him.

crossReferences.why: Shows the same obstruction from the other side: a man forbidden while he is praying.
Another instruction about how God is to be called upon, given in the same Meccan pressure.
Names the places where God's name is mentioned as what divine defence preserves.

studies.applyIt: Next time you pray, notice the moment your forehead reaches the floor and nothing in the room is in front of you any more. One classical reading of this passage says that patch of floor is what the word covers, not the building around it. Pick one prayer today and perform it slowly enough to register that second.

studies.title: No Shelter Except With Him
studies.meaning: Two disclaimers, and the second is much harder than the first. He is told to say that he controls neither of the two things people want from a figure of authority: the power to hurt them and the power to put them right. Then the disclaimer turns inward. The same man has no protector against God either, and the only shelter there is runs toward the one he would be sheltering from. The word for that shelter names a place you turn aside into, so the sentence describes a direction rather than a bargain.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the years when the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) had lost the clan backing that had kept him safe and was negotiating for formal protection in order to move about the valley at all. The surrounding ayat answer people who wanted a demonstration of power from him. The sources report the search for a guarantor in some detail and agree that it was refused more than once before a grant was made.

keyTerms.note: The verb of ownership used for capability. To own a thing is to dispose of it, so denying ownership of harm and of guidance denies any standing to hand out either one.

The verb for taking a neighbour under your formal guarantee, a defined arrangement in Arabian society with witnesses and consequences. Denying that anyone can do it removes the surest safety a man of that world could obtain.
A noun of place from a root meaning to turn aside. It names the hollow you swerve into off an open road. It occurs twice in the Quran and both times inside a denial.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Protection was the Meccan safety net, and it could be withdrawn. A man with no clan behind him could be killed without consequence, and an outsider entering the valley needed a citizen to vouch for him before he could trade or sleep there. The arrangement was announced publicly and held even when the protector disliked the man's cause. The word in the second of these ayat is that arrangement's technical term.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a place of refuge here occurs in only one other ayah of the Quran, closing an instruction to recite what has been revealed and stating that nothing can alter God's words. Both times it arrives at the end of a sentence and both times it is denied: apart from God, no such place is to be found.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage strips the Prophet of every capacity that would make him worth flattering or worth fearing on his own account. He cannot harm, he cannot guide, and he has no cover of his own to offer or to shelter under. What is left is the work of carrying a message, which the next ayah names. This is one of the places where the Quran keeps prophecy from turning into patronage, and it does so by putting the words in his own mouth.

crossReferences.why: Has him disclaim power over his own harm and benefit in almost identical wording.
Uses the same rare word for refuge, closing a passage on holding fast to what was revealed.
Extends the disclaimer to knowledge of the unseen and to his own gain and loss alike.

studies.applyIt: Think of the person you most want to change: a child, a sibling, a friend who is drifting. Say to yourself once, in plain words, that bringing them to right conduct is not in your power. Then do the one thing that is. Make the call, cook the meal, leave the door open. The disclaimer is not permission to give up. It is what keeps you from despairing.

studies.title: Nothing But The Delivery
studies.meaning: The exception attaches to the sentence before it and states what the Prophet does have, since the previous ayah has just stripped him of shelter and of power. What he has is a delivery: an announcement from God, and the individual messages that make it up. The grammar has been argued over, because the exception can be read as continuing either the refuge clause or the disclaimer, and the commentators lay out the range. The consequence named afterwards belongs to God and not to the messenger, which keeps the division of labour intact.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The ayah closes a run of instructed speeches given while the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was being pressed for a demonstration of authority, and it answers by narrowing his office rather than widening it. No specific occasion is reported. The setting is a community small enough that the question of what its founder could actually do for people was being asked out loud.

keyTerms.note: A verbal noun from the verb for reaching a destination. It names the act of getting something there intact, not its content and not its effect, which is exactly the portion assigned to a messenger.
A plural, where the Quran often uses a singular for revelation as a whole. The plural treats it as a series of dispatches carried over years rather than as one finished book handed across.
The root means lasting without change more than lasting without end; Arabic used it of long-lived things generally. The following word for perpetuity is what fixes the sense here.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A messenger was a defined and limited office. A clan sent a man with a formal announcement to another clan, he delivered the wording he had been given, and he was not answerable for how it landed. His safety depended on that understanding being honoured by both sides. Errands like this crossed the desert constantly, carrying terms, refusals, marriage offers and news of deaths. The word used here is the ordinary one for that job.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for delivering a message and the verb for reaching a destination share one root, and the Quran uses that root in strikingly physical places: a child reaching the age of marriage, and the soul reaching the throat at the moment of death. The same verb that describes a message arriving describes a life arriving at its edge.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah draws a hard line under what a prophet is for. He carries, and the carrying is finished when the words arrive; what happens after that is neither his work nor his failure. That protects the message from being judged by how many accept it, and it protects the messenger from the two temptations of the office, which are taking credit for belief and taking rejection personally.

crossReferences.why: States the messenger's whole duty as delivery and leaves everything else to God's knowledge.
Separates delivery from outcome explicitly: yours is to convey, ours is to reckon.
Assigns the messenger his load and the hearers theirs, using the same vocabulary of carrying.

studies.applyIt: Think of something true you said once to somebody who did not take it. A warning, an apology, an offer of help. You have been quietly keeping score of the result ever since. Today, try counting only the delivery. Whether it landed was never the part you were holding.

studies.title: Weaker In Helpers, Fewer In Number
studies.meaning: The first sentence answers a taunt without repeating it. Mecca's case against the small community was arithmetic, that they had more men and better backing, and the reply does not dispute the count. It dates it. Then the Prophet is made to say that he does not know when the promised thing arrives, or whether a long term will be set for it. The force of the passage comes from that pairing: certainty about what, declared ignorance about when, stated by the one person the audience assumed had been told.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the years when the believers were few enough to be counted by name and the jeer about their numbers was in the air. The surrounding surahs record the same objection in several forms, that a message with so little backing could not be from God. Commentators read these ayat as an answer to it. No particular occasion is reported; the setting is the ordinary pressure on a movement that was visibly outnumbered.

keyTerms.note: Singular where English wants a plural, a common Arabic way of counting a category rather than individuals. The word belongs to tribal alliance: the men obliged to turn out when you call them.

keyTerms.gloss: a term, a stretch of time
keyTerms.note: It names an extent that has an end, not a point on a calendar. Saying God may set one makes the delay itself deliberate rather than evidence that nothing is coming.
A noun for what is absent from perception rather than for what is mysterious in itself. The definite form turns it into a domain, and the clause that follows closes that domain to every creature.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Strength was counted out loud. Genealogies were recited to establish how many fighting men a clan could raise, and poets made the tally itself a boast, naming allies and numbering spears. A small group with few backers had no standing in that arithmetic, whatever the merits of its case. The objection behind this passage was not an insult in that world. It was an argument, and it was thought to be a good one.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran has the Prophet disclaim knowledge of when the promise falls due in several places, and every time the disclaimer is introduced by the imperative to say it. It is never reported as a remark he offered; it is issued to him as wording. Four of the last nine ayat of this surah begin with that same imperative.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two kinds of not knowing are distinguished in three ayat. The Prophet's ignorance of the timing is a fact about him. The closing sentence makes it a fact about creation, describing the unseen as God's own possession rather than as a store of information that rank might unlock. Access is not a privilege that can be earned. The following ayah will qualify this for messengers, but the default stated here is complete exclusion.

crossReferences.why: Puts the same question about timing to him and supplies the same instructed answer.
Describes the keys of the unseen as held by God alone, with nothing outside that reach.
Repeats the question about the Hour and hands it back unanswered, in a Medinan setting.

studies.applyIt: Count something today that you have been letting stand as an impression: how many people actually back the thing you are doing, or how many days you have really kept at it. Then notice how little the number decides. This passage never denies that its audience was outnumbered. It says only that the count was taken too early.

studies.title: Guards Before Him And Behind
studies.meaning: The exclusion stated a moment earlier is opened by exactly one door, and even that door is watched. A messenger God has approved receives some of what is hidden, and an escort is posted in front of him and behind him around the transmission itself. The purpose clause has occupied commentators, since God's knowledge is not acquired; they read it as knowledge made manifest, or as the messenger's own certainty that the delivery arrived whole. The surah then closes by counting everything, which is the same guarantee restated as arithmetic.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. These are the last two ayat of the surah, and they answer the question the previous ones raised: if the unseen is closed to everyone, how does any of this reach a human being at all. The setting is a Mecca where rival claims to hidden knowledge were commercially available, and where the difference between a prophet and a soothsayer was the live question about the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him).

keyTerms.gloss: He approved, He was pleased with
keyTerms.note: A verb of acceptance rather than selection on merit. The form carries settled satisfaction, so the messenger is described as somebody God is pleased with, not as somebody who qualified for the post.
The same word used earlier in this surah for what lies in wait above the heads of eavesdroppers. One term covers the guard that keeps the unseen shut and the guard that keeps a revelation intact.
From the root for pebbles, which is how counts were kept. The verb means holding an exact number rather than a general grasp, and it lands on the last line of the surah.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Dispatches that mattered travelled with an escort. A letter carrying terms between clans went with riders ahead and behind, because the danger to a message was not only theft. A word altered in transit was far harder to detect than a message that never arrived, and a courier who could be got at privately was worth more to an enemy than one who could be robbed. The picture in these ayat is a guarded column, and the audience had watched them ride out.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the posted watch here has already appeared in this surah, back where flames lie in wait for anyone listening at the edge of the sky. The same term serves the guard that keeps the unseen closed and the guard that keeps a revelation whole. The surah then ends on a word for number, having opened with a band small enough to count.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Revelation is presented as a secured channel rather than as inspiration welling up. The content is God's, the carrier is chosen rather than qualified, and the route is watched at both ends, which makes the integrity of the message a divine undertaking instead of a human achievement. The final clause then extends that precision to everything there is, so the care taken over one transmission turns out to be the ordinary way God holds what exists.

crossReferences.why: States the same rule and the same exception: the unseen is closed, but messengers are chosen.
Makes the safeguarding of the revelation something God undertakes directly, not the community.
Describes the carrier of the revelation as strong, trusted and obeyed where he stands.

studies.applyIt: Pass something on exactly today. A message from one person to another, a set of instructions, an account of somebody who is not in the room. Do not improve it, trim it for effect, or soften the part that will not be welcome. Notice how strong the pull to adjust it is, and how much of that pull is about you rather than about them.
